title: Comparing things, and the weather
goal: Compare anything with anything — bigger, cheaper, the best — and talk about the two seasons Indonesia actually has, which is the small talk you will make most often.
bekal: talk about rain, heat and the two seasons
make the kind of easy small talk that starts conversations

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Musim hujan
dialogs.intro: The rain has been coming down for an hour. Sarah and Pak Slamet are stuck under the awning of the warung.

lines.speaker: Slamet:
lines.text: Deras sekali, ya. Sudah musim hujan.
lines.id: It's really coming down. The rainy season's here.
lines.literal: heavy very, yes. already season rain.

lines.speaker: Slamet:
lines.text: Di Australia ada musim hujan juga?
lines.id: Do you have a rainy season in Australia?
lines.literal: at Australia exist season rain also?

lines.speaker: Slamet:
lines.text: Empat? Wah. Dingin sekali di sana?
lines.id: Four? Goodness. Is it very cold there?
lines.literal: four? wow. cold very at there?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Musim dingin lebih dingin daripada di sini, jauh.
lines.id: Winter is much colder than here.
lines.literal: season cold more cold than at here, far.

lines.speaker: Slamet:
lines.text: Saya tidak tahan dingin. Di sini paling enak.
lines.id: I can't stand the cold. Here is the nicest.
lines.literal: I not endure cold. at here most pleasant.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Tapi Jakarta panas sekali, Pak. Bandung lebih sejuk.
lines.id: But Jakarta is very hot. Bandung is cooler.
lines.literal: but Jakarta hot very, Mr. Bandung more cool.

lines.speaker: Slamet:
lines.text: Betul. Bandung sama sejuknya dengan Bogor.
lines.id: True. Bandung is as cool as Bogor.
lines.literal: correct. Bandung same cool-its with Bogor.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: When does the rainy season end?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Masih lama. Untung saya bawa payung.
lines.id: A long way to go, then. Lucky I brought an umbrella.
lines.literal: still long. lucky I bring umbrella.

notes: **Lebih … daripada is the whole comparative.** *Lebih dingin daripada* — "more cold than". The adjective never changes: there is no *colder*, no *coldest*, no irregular forms to learn. 💬 In speech *daripada* is often shortened to *dari*: *lebih dingin dari di sini*.

**Paling means "most".** *Paling enak* (the nicest), *paling murah* (the cheapest), *paling dekat* (the nearest). There is also a prefix *ter-* doing the same job — *termurah*, *terbaik* — which you will see in advertising and headlines more than you will hear in speech.

**Sama … dengan — "as … as".** The pattern is *sama* + adjective + *-nya* + *dengan*: *sama sejuknya dengan* (as cool as). It looks fussy but is fixed, and *sama mahalnya dengan* will get you through most of it.

**Indonesia has two seasons, not four.** *Musim hujan* (rainy, roughly October to April) and *musim kemarau* (dry). Temperature barely changes all year; what changes is how wet it is. Explaining your own four seasons will be a recurring conversation, and *musim dingin*, *musim panas*, *musim semi*, *musim gugur* are the words you will need.

**Tidak tahan — "can't stand it".** *Tahan* means to endure or withstand: *tahan panas* (can take heat), *tidak tahan pedas* (can't handle spicy food). That last one may become your most-used sentence in the country.

grammars.title: The three comparisons
body: Everything you need, in one table.
after: *Kurang* is the quiet star of this table. You met it in Unit 6 as the polite softener, and here it is again: *kurang enak* is "not quite nice" rather than "bad", *kurang besar* is "a bit small". Indonesians reach for it constantly.
To intensify a comparison, add *jauh* (far) or *sedikit* (a little): *jauh lebih dingin* (far colder), *sedikit lebih mahal* (slightly more expensive).

grammars.title: Weather
body: Weather sentences need no verb and often no subject at all: *Panas* is a complete remark.
after: Two facts worth knowing about Indonesian rain. It usually arrives in the afternoon and it usually stops — sheltering for twenty minutes is normal behaviour, and every warung expects it. And *banjir* is not an exotic word in Jakarta: streets flood several times a season, and *Jalan itu banjir* is ordinary traffic news.

blocks.text: Weather, traffic, food and where you are going are the four safe subjects, and Indonesians open with them constantly. These lines will start more conversations than any grammar in this book.

head: Indonesian
English
rows: Have you been in Indonesia long?
Are you happy here? / Do you like it here?

blocks.text: **Betah** has no English equivalent: it means to feel at home somewhere, to be content to stay. *Betah di sini?* is a genuinely warm question, and the answer *Betah!* will please whoever asked it.

And the last two lines are a script. Your Indonesian will be praised long before it is good; the expected answer is modest — *masih belajar*, *belum lancar*, *sedikit-sedikit* (just a little). Accepting the compliment outright is not wrong, but deflecting it is what Indonesians do.

sections.title: Islands, cities and where you are

blocks.text: Indonesia is bigger than most visitors expect: from Aceh in the north-west to Papua in the east is roughly the distance from London to Kabul, and it crosses three time zones. *Dari Sabang sampai Merauke* — from the westernmost town to the easternmost — is the phrase every Indonesian schoolchild learns for it.

exercises.prompt: Compare the two, using lebih and the adjective in brackets.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: Bandung lebih sejuk daripada Jakarta. — Yang ini lebih murah. — Yang mana paling murah? — Sama mahalnya dengan yang itu. — Setiap sore hujan. — Saya tidak tahan pedas. — Sudah lama di Indonesia?
